skills.name: Describe the occurrence and properties of nitrogen

note.text:
Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of the air by volume. It is also combined in proteins, in nitrates in the soil, and in ammonia.
Laboratory preparation from air: remove carbon dioxide with sodium hydroxide, dry the air, then pass it over heated copper, which takes the oxygen. What is left is nitrogen with a little argon, so it is slightly denser than pure nitrogen.
Pure nitrogen is made by heating ammonium nitrite: NH4NO2 → N2 + 2H2O.
In industry it comes from the fractional distillation of liquid air.
Properties: a colourless, odourless gas, almost insoluble in water, slightly less dense than air, and very unreactive because of the strong triple bond N≡N. It does not burn and does not support burning. It combines with magnesium (3Mg + N2 → Mg3N2), with hydrogen in the Haber process, and with oxygen in a lightning flash.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to say where nitrogen is found, prepare it from air, and explain its properties from its triple bond.
Builds on: Form One the composition of air, and Form Three bonding.
Leads to: Lesson {12} (ammonia) and Lesson {16}, the nitrogen cycle.

sections.heading: Where nitrogen is found, and how it is obtained
sections.text:
Nitrogen makes up about {78} per cent of the air by volume. It is also combined in the proteins of living things, in nitrates in the soil, and in ammonia.
From air in the laboratory: pass air through sodium hydroxide solution to take out carbon dioxide, then through concentrated sulphuric acid to dry it, then over heated copper, which takes the oxygen:
{2}Cu + {formula('O2')} → {2}{formula('CuO')}
What is left is nitrogen with a little argon, so it is slightly DENSER than pure nitrogen.
Pure nitrogen: heat ammonium nitrite, {formula('NH4NO2')} → {formula('N2')} + {2}{formula('H2O')}.
In industry: fractional distillation of liquid air, where nitrogen boils off first.

sections.heading: Properties
sections.text:
Nitrogen is a colourless, odourless gas, almost insoluble in water, and very slightly less dense than air (relative molecular mass {28} against about {29} for air).
It is very unreactive. Its two atoms are joined by a TRIPLE bond, N≡N, which needs a great deal of energy to break. It does not burn and does not support burning.
It does react in hard conditions:
• with burning magnesium: {3}Mg + {formula('N2')} → {formula('Mg3N2')};
• with hydrogen under pressure and a catalyst (the Haber process): {formula('N2')} + {3}{formula('H2')} → {2}{formula('NH3')};
• with oxygen in a lightning flash or a hot engine: {formula('N2')} + {formula('O2')} → {2}{formula('NO')}.
Being unreactive makes it useful: packets of food and oil tanks are filled with it to keep oxygen out.

mistake.wrong: nitrogen is unreactive because its atoms have full outer shells
mistake.right: it is unreactive because of the strong triple bond
mistake.why: A nitrogen ATOM has {5} outer electrons. It is the N≡N bond in the molecule that is hard to break.

worked_example.problem: Explain why nitrogen obtained by removing oxygen from air is slightly denser than nitrogen made from ammonium nitrite.
steps: Removing carbon dioxide, water and oxygen from air leaves nitrogen and the noble gases.
The noble gases, mainly argon, are not removed by heated copper.
Argon has a relative atomic mass of {40}, well above the {28} of a nitrogen molecule.
So the mixture is a little denser than pure nitrogen.
worked_example.answer: because it still contains argon, which is denser than nitrogen

pick.q: About what fraction of the air is nitrogen by volume?
pick.r: About {78} per cent
e: {21} per cent is the proportion of oxygen.
Nitrogen is far more than half of the air.
Less than {1} per cent covers argon, carbon dioxide and the rest together.
pick.y: Air is about {78} per cent nitrogen, {21} per cent oxygen and {1} per cent other gases by volume.

pick.r: Its two atoms are held by a strong triple bond that is hard to break
w: Its atoms have a full outer shell already
e: A nitrogen atom has {5} outer electrons, so it is not full; the molecule is stable because of the bond.
Nitrogen is in group {5}, not group {0}; it is not a noble gas.
The molecule is small; it is the strength of the bond that matters.
pick.y: A great deal of energy is needed to break the N≡N triple bond, so nitrogen reacts only in hard conditions.

pick.q: How can nitrogen be obtained from air in the laboratory?
pick.r: By passing air over heated copper to remove the oxygen, after removing carbon dioxide and water
w: By cooling air until the nitrogen freezes out
By bubbling air through sodium hydroxide only
e: Air cannot be burned; something must be burned IN it.
That is the industrial method (fractional distillation of liquid air), not the laboratory one.
Sodium hydroxide removes carbon dioxide only, leaving the oxygen behind.
pick.y: Heated copper takes the oxygen as copper(II) oxide, leaving nitrogen with a little argon.

pick.q: Nitrogen prepared from air is slightly denser than pure nitrogen. Why?
pick.r: It still contains the noble gases, mainly argon, which are denser
w: Nitrogen from air has heavier atoms
e: The oxygen has been removed by the heated copper.
The air is dried before the oxygen is removed.
Atoms of nitrogen from air are the same as any other nitrogen atoms.
pick.y: Argon and the other noble gases are not removed, and argon has a relative atomic mass of {40}.

pick.q: Magnesium burns in nitrogen. What is formed?
pick.r: Magnesium nitride, {formula('Mg3N2')}
w: Magnesium and nitrogen do not react
e: Magnesium oxide needs oxygen, which is not present here.
Magnesium is reactive enough to combine with nitrogen when it is burning.
Ammonia needs hydrogen as well; it is not formed directly here.
pick.y: {3}Mg + {formula('N2')} → {formula('Mg3N2')}: one of the few reactions of nitrogen at ordinary pressure.

pick.q: How is nitrogen obtained in industry?
pick.r: By the fractional distillation of liquid air
w: By passing air over heated copper
e: Heating nitrates gives oxygen and oxides of nitrogen, not pure nitrogen.
Natural gas is mainly methane; it is a source of hydrogen, not nitrogen.
That is the laboratory method and is far too slow for industry.
pick.y: Air is liquefied and then distilled; nitrogen boils off first at −{196} °C, before oxygen at −{183} °C.
